title: Week 6 Notes: Feature Engineering
text:
A linear model draws straight lines through the features it receives. Feature engineering changes or adds predictors so that a linear model can represent skew, curves, group differences, and place-level variation.
The lecture evaluates changes by cross-validated RMSE, not by p-values. To compare models fairly, use the same observations and the same cross-validation folds throughout.








Feature change
What it can do for predictions
How to read coefficients




Log
Handle skew and nonlinear scaling
Often changes the unit to a percentage interpretation


Squared term
Let a relationship curve
The linear and squared terms must be interpreted together


Category
Represent groups or jumps
Each coefficient compares a group to a reference


Interaction
Let a slope vary by group
The effect depends on the group


Fixed effect
Account for unmeasured differences among places
Describes adjusted place differences; it does not explain their causes

title: Week 6 Notes: Feature Engineering
text:
3.1 Why log?
Income and rent can be right-skewed. A few very high values can pull a straight-line fit. A log compresses the upper tail and makes equal percentage changes comparable distances. For example, moving from $20,000 to $40,000 may matter more than moving from $180,000 to $200,000, even though both changes are $20,000.

3.1.1 Log a predictor
f_logx <- rent ~ log(income) + pct_renter + bldg_age + dist_ch_mi
m_logx <- lm(f_logx, data = tracts)

b <- coef(m_logx)["log(income)"]
b / 100             # approximate rent change for a 1% income increase
b * log(1.10)       # exact model-implied change for a 10% increase
In a level–log model (y ~ log(x)), a 1% increase in x is associated with approximately β / 100 units of y, holding other variables constant.

title: Week 6 Notes: Feature Engineering
text:
3.2 Zeros: log1p()
log(0) is negative infinity. This causes problems for variables that can be zero, such as counts of crimes, trees, or 311 calls. Use log1p(x), which calculates log(x + 1):
log1p(c(0, 1, 10, 100))
The percentage interpretation is approximate, especially for small values.

title: Week 6 Notes: Feature Engineering
text:
3.3 Log the outcome
f_logy <- log(rent) ~ log(income) + pct_renter + bldg_age + dist_ch_mi
m_logy <- lm(f_logy, data = tracts)
In a log–level model (log(y) ~ x), a one-unit increase in x is associated with approximately 100 × β percent change in y. For a larger coefficient, calculate the exact percentage as (exp(β) - 1) × 100.
In a log–log model (log(y) ~ log(x)), β is an elasticity: a 1% increase in x is associated with approximately a β% change in y.







Model form
Approximate coefficient interpretation




Level–level: y ~ x
+1 unit of x → β units of y


Level–log: y ~ log(x)
+1% of x → β / 100 units of y


Log–level: log(y) ~ x
+1 unit of x → about 100 × β% change in y


Log–log: log(y) ~ log(x)
+1% of x → about β% change in y



RMSE trap: RMSE must be on the same outcome scale to compare models. A residual RMSE from a model of log(rent) is in log-dollars; it cannot be compared with the baseline RMSE in dollars. During cross-validation, exponentiate predictions before calculating RMSE. Directly exponentiating a predicted log often estimates closer to the median than the mean, so it can underpredict somewhat; the lecture treats this simple back-transformation as adequate for the assignment.

title: Week 6 Notes: Feature Engineering
text:
7.1 Fixed effects and cross-validation
A fixed effect can only predict groups represented in the training data. If a district is absent from a training fold, its coefficient is unavailable and prediction can fail. Count group sizes before cross-validation. The lecture’s rule of thumb is around 10 or more observations per group for 10-fold CV, with more being safer.
Possible responses to very small groups:

Merge them with a geographically or substantively sensible neighbor (preferred when defensible).
Lump small groups into “Other” for a quick solution, while recognizing the group may combine unrelated places.
Use a coarser geography.

The example merges small districts with nearby districts for the CV predictor. It emphasizes that FE is a kind of place memorization and cannot generalize to a never-seen place.







Fixed effects
Spatial features




Capture unmeasured differences associated with a group
Represent measured conditions such as proximity to transit, parks, or crime


Cannot predict an unseen group
Can be computed wherever the feature is available


Group boundaries and scale are inherited
Feature scale can be chosen


Tell you where adjusted differences are
Help describe what may explain differences



They can complement each other: spatial features explain measured conditions, while FE can account for remaining place-level differences.

library(tidyverse)
library(tidycensus)
library(sf)
library(caret)     # cross-validation

section: Part 1: Rebuild the table you already know
text:
Part 1: Rebuild the table you already know
This is last week’s pull with a few more variables. Every line should look familiar.

philly_tracts <- get_acs(
  geography = "tract",
  state = "PA",
  county = "Philadelphia",
  variables = c(
    med_rent   = "B25064_001",   # median gross rent (our Y)
    med_inc    = "B19013_001",   # median household income
    total_pop  = "B01003_001",
    occ_units  = "B25003_001",   # occupied housing units
    renter_occ = "B25003_003",   # renter-occupied units
    edu_total  = "B15003_001",   # population 25+
    ba         = "B15003_022",
    ma         = "B15003_023",
    prof       = "B15003_024",
    phd        = "B15003_025"
  ),
  year = 2023,
  output = "wide",
  geometry = TRUE
) %>%
  st_transform(2272)          # Pennsylvania South State Plane, feet

Now build the variables. A data frame goes in, a data frame comes out.

philly_tracts <- philly_tracts %>%
  mutate(
    pct_renter = renter_occE / occ_unitsE * 100,
    pct_ba     = (baE + maE + profE + phdE) / edu_totalE * 100,
    rent_se    = med_rentM / 1.645,
    rent_cv    = rent_se / renter_occE * 100
  )

Bring back the stations and count how many sit within half a mile of each tract. This is Week 4 with one new function.

stations <- st_read("https://www.rideindego.com/stations/json/", quiet = TRUE) %>%
  st_transform(st_crs(philly_tracts))

philly_tracts <- philly_tracts %>%
  mutate(n_stations = lengths(st_is_within_distance(., stations, dist = 2640)))

Stop and look: st_is_within_distance() returns a list, one element per tract, holding the stations within range. What does lengths() do to that list?

Which tracts can we model?
A regression can’t use a row with a missing Y or X. R will quietly drop those rows, and later your residuals won’t line up with your tracts. So drop them yourself, on purpose, and count.

nrow(philly_tracts)

tracts <- philly_tracts %>%
  filter(total_popE > 0,
         !is.na(med_rentE),
         !is.na(med_incE),
         !is.na(pct_ba),
         !is.na(pct_renter))

nrow(tracts)

Rule from Week 4, again: how many tracts did you lose? Which kind of tract has no median rent? (Hint: think about who lives there.)

Part 4: Read the same output twice
Add the other predictors.

m2 <- lm(med_rentE ~ med_incE + pct_renter + pct_ba + n_stations, data = tracts)
summary(m2)

Look at the n_stations coefficient. Answer both questions in one or two sentences each:

β̂ reading: Can you tell the housing agency that bike share stations raise rents? Why or why not?
Your answer:

Your answer:







NoteSame number, two questions

title: Week 5 In-Class Lab: Where the Model Is Wrong
text:
Part 5: Uncertainty in input data
Our Y is an ACS estimate with its own margin of error. Add the residuals to the table and check whether the biggest misses happen where the estimate is least reliable.

tracts <- tracts %>%
  mutate(fitted_m2 = fitted(m2),
         resid_m2  = residuals(___))

ggplot(tracts, aes(x = rent_cv, y = abs(resid_m2))) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.5) +
  geom_smooth(se = FALSE) +
  labs(x = "CV of the median rent estimate (%)",
       y = "Size of the model's miss ($)",
       title = "Are the biggest misses in the noisiest tracts?") +
  theme_minimal()

Stop and look: If a tract’s rent estimate has a CV of 35%, how much of the model’s miss there could be survey noise rather than a model failure? What does that mean for flagging “tracts with rents above expectation”?

title: Week 5 In-Class Lab: Where the Model Is Wrong
text:
Part 6: Fit vs. prediction






WarningTwo different CVs



Week 3 CV = coefficient of variation: how noisy is one estimate? Today’s CV = cross-validation: how well does a model predict data it hasn’t seen? Same letters, unrelated ideas.



6A: One train/test split

set.seed(5080)
n <- nrow(tracts)
train_idx <- sample(1:n, size = 0.8 * n)

train_data <- tracts[train_idx, ]
test_data  <- tracts[___, ]

m2_train <- lm(med_rentE ~ med_incE + pct_renter + pct_ba + n_stations,
               data = train_data)

test_pred <- predict(m2_train, newdata = ___)

rmse_train <- sqrt(mean(residuals(m2_train)^2))
rmse_test  <- sqrt(mean((test_data$med_rentE - test_pred)^2))

c(train = rmse_train, test = rmse_test)

Stop and look: Which RMSE is larger? Why would you expect that? In words: “The model’s typical miss on tracts it hasn’t seen is about $___ per month.”
Change the seed to any other number and rerun the chunk. Did the test RMSE change? That’s why one split isn’t enough.


6B: 10-fold cross-validation
caret wants a plain data frame, so drop the geometry first. (The geometry isn’t a predictor, and train() will choke on it.)

model_df <- tracts %>% st_drop_geometry()

ctrl <- trainControl(method = "cv", number = ___)

set.seed(5080)
cv_m1 <- train(med_rentE ~ med_incE,
               data = model_df, method = "lm", trControl = ctrl)

set.seed(5080)
cv_m2 <- train(med_rentE ~ med_incE + pct_renter + pct_ba + n_stations,
               data = model_df, method = "lm", trControl = ctrl)

cv_m1$results
cv_m2$results

Setting the same seed before each train() gives both models the same folds, so the comparison is fair.
Stop and look: Fill in the table.




In-sample R²
CV RMSE




m1




m2





Did adding variables improve R²? Did it improve CV RMSE by as much? For a prediction task, which column is the grade?

title: Week 5 In-Class Lab: Where the Model Is Wrong
section: Part 7: Where is the model wrong?
text:
Part 7: Where is the model wrong?

7A: Residuals vs. fitted

ggplot(tracts, aes(x = fitted_m2, y = resid_m2)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.5) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, color = "red") +
  labs(x = "Predicted rent", y = "Residual (actual − predicted)") +
  theme_minimal()

bptest(m2)

Stop and look: Random cloud, funnel, or curve? If it’s a funnel, the predictions aren’t biased, but one RMSE hides the fact that the model misses by much more in some tracts. Which tracts?


7B: The map
The residuals are already a column in an sf data frame. Mapping them is one geom_sf() away.

ggplot(tracts) +
  geom_sf(aes(fill = ___), color = NA) +
  scale_fill_gradient2(low = "#2166ac", mid = "grey95", high = "#b2182b",
                       midpoint = 0, labels = scales::dollar) +
  theme_void() +
  labs(title = "Where the rent model is wrong",
       subtitle = "Red = rent higher than predicted · Blue = lower than predicted",
       fill = "Residual")

Stop and look: If the errors were random, the map would look speckled. Does it? Where do the reds sit together? What might those places have in common that the model doesn’t know about?
Write down your answer. We’ll come back to it in Weeks 6 and 7.

title: Week 5 In-Class Lab: Where the Model Is Wrong
text:
Part 8: The Challenge
Your team’s job: build the best model for predicting tract median rent, then use it to answer the agency’s question.

Rules

The grade is 10-fold CV RMSE. Use model_df (or tracts) and run set.seed(5080) directly before train(), exactly as in Part 6B, so every team is tested on the same folds.
Don’t drop rows. If you add a variable with missing values, you change the folds and the comparison stops being fair. Fill the gaps or choose a different variable.
You may add any ACS variables (use load_variables(2023, "acs5") to browse) and any spatial feature you can build with Week 4 tools: distances, buffers, counts.
You may not use anything built from rent itself. That rules out med_rentM, rent_cv, rent burden (B25071), and the rent distribution tables (B25063). Ask yourself: would the agency have this variable for a tract whose rent it’s trying to predict? If not, using it is cheating the test. That’s called leakage.



Deliver

Your CV RMSE, in dollars, written as a sentence.
One feature you added, and why. What did you think it would capture that the census variables miss? Did it help?
One coefficient, read twice. Pick a variable in your final model and give its β̂ reading and its ŷ reading in one sentence each.
The agency’s list. Using your final model fit to all tracts, find the five tracts with the largest positive residuals (rent well above expectation). For each, report the residual and the rent CV. Which of the five would you tell the agency to trust, and which might be fog?
Your residual map. Did your added features make the clusters from Part 7B shrink?


# Your team's code here



Scoring (for bragging rights, not grades)




Points




Lowest CV RMSE in the room
3


Second and third lowest
2 / 1


Feature explanation is clear and specific
2


Coefficient read correctly both ways
2


Agency list accounts for reliability (Week 3)
2


Randomly chosen presenter explains the model clearly
3


Breaks a rule (leakage or dropped rows)
−5





Before you present, discuss

One of your variables is not statistically significant, but removing it makes CV RMSE worse. Do you keep it? What would your Spatial Statistics instructor say, and why is neither of you wrong?
A council member sees your model and says, “So your model proves that renters drive up rents.” What do you say?
If the agency uses your top-five list to target inspections, whose rents does a model error hurt most?

title: Assignment 4: Building Features, Watching What Happens
text:
This is not a competition. There’s no leaderboard and no target RMSE. The goal is to practice the full prediction workflow on a question you choose, and to find out what actually helps. Some features you’re sure will help won’t, and some you add on a whim will. Both are findings.
You’ll:

Choose a tract-level outcome for Philadelphia and check whether it’s reliable enough to model (Weeks 2–3).
Fit a baseline model and cross-validate it (Week 5).
Pull data from Philadelphia’s open data portal through its API and build spatial features: counts, densities, and distances (Week 4, plus one new tool).
Transform variables with logs, squared terms, and categories. Watch the October 9 recorded lecture before Part 5.
Keep a model log the whole way through, and compare where your first and final models go wrong.

Timing. Parts 1–4 use only what we’ve covered through Week 5. You can finish them before the October 9 lecture. Part 5 is new material; the lecture explains it, and the instructions below give you the essentials.
Type the code yourself. The worked examples show the pattern. Your job is to apply it to your outcome and your data choices.








Important1. Don’t drop rows



Every model is cross-validated on the same tracts with the same folds, so the rows in your model log are comparable. If a new variable has missing values, fill them (for example, 0 for a count, or the median with a note) or choose a different variable. The cv_rmse() helper below will stop and tell you if you break this rule.


Your outcome comes from the 2019–2023 ACS. Pull open data from 2023 or earlier (2021–2023 is ideal). Using 2025 data to predict a 2023 outcome uses information from the future, which a real prediction model would never have.



Don’t use any variable that’s built from your outcome or measures the same thing another way. Ask yourself: would an agency trying to predict this outcome for a tract have this variable? If the answer is “only because it’s basically the outcome,” leave it out.

title: Assignment 4: Predicting Philadelphia’s Mean Commute Time
text:
I ask whether tract-level income, education, population density, commute mode, centrality, and recent public-safety context help predict mean commute time among Philadelphia workers who do not work from home. The outcome is ACS B08013_001 (aggregate travel time to work) divided by B08303_001 (commuting workers), in minutes. Both ACS estimates describe workers age 16 and over who did not work from home. This is an observed commute-duration measure, not a direct measure of how many jobs a person can reach. All models are exploratory predictions, not causal estimates.
I use three ACS predictors in the baseline—median household income, bachelor’s attainment, and population density. I then test commuter mode shares from ACS B08301, spatial features from 2023 city records, distance from City Hall, a distance ring, and Philadelphia planning-district fixed effects. I do not use either commute-time table estimate as a predictor because those would directly reconstruct the outcome.

title: Assignment 4: Building Features, Watching What Happens
text:
Part 0: Setup


Code
library(tidyverse)
library(tidycensus)
library(sf)
library(caret)

Sys.getenv("CENSUS_API_KEY") != ""   # should print TRUE


[1] TRUE



The cross-validation helper
This function runs 10-fold cross-validation with the same seed every time, so every model in your log is tested on the same folds. You don’t need to change it. Read it once so you know what it does.


Code
ctrl <- trainControl(method = "cv", number = 10)

cv_rmse <- function(formula, data) {
  df <- if (inherits(data, "sf")) st_drop_geometry(data) else data
  vars <- all.vars(formula)
  bad <- vars[sapply(vars, function(v) any(is.na(df[[v]])))]
  if (length(bad) > 0) {
    stop("These variables have NAs: ", paste(bad, collapse = ", "),
         ". Fill them or choose another variable (Rule 1: don't drop rows).")
  }
  set.seed(5080)
  fit <- train(formula, data = df, method = "lm", trControl = ctrl)
  fit$results$RMSE
}




The model log
Every time you fit a new model, add a row. By the end, this table is the story of your assignment.


Code
model_log <- tibble(
  model   = character(),
  added   = character(),
  cv_rmse = numeric(),
  notes   = character()
)

title: Assignment 4: Predicting Philadelphia’s Mean Commute Time
section: Part 1: Choose and check the outcome
text:
Part 1: Choose and check the outcome

1A. Pull ACS estimates and construct variables
The baseline predictors are median household income (B19013), bachelor’s degree attainment among adults 25 and over (B15003), and population density (B01003 divided by tract area). I also obtain public-transit and drove-alone counts (B08301), then divide them by B08303_001 so both are commuter shares for workers who did not work from home.


Show code
philly_tracts <- get_acs(
  geography = "tract", state = "PA", county = "Philadelphia",
  variables = c(
    total_pop = "B01003_001",
    total_commute_minutes = "B08013_001",
    commuting_workers = "B08303_001",
    median_income = "B19013_001",
    adult_population = "B15003_001",
    bachelors = "B15003_022",
    drove_alone = "B08301_003",
    public_transit = "B08301_010"
  ),
  year = 2023, survey = "acs5", output = "wide", geometry = TRUE
) %>%
  st_transform(2272) %>%
  mutate(
    y = total_commute_minutesE / commuting_workersE,
    y_moe = moe_ratio(total_commute_minutesE, commuting_workersE,
                      total_commute_minutesM, commuting_workersM),
    y_cv = if_else(y > 0, (y_moe / 1.645) / y * 100, NA_real_),
    area_sqmi = as.numeric(st_area(geometry)) / 27878400,
    pop_density = total_popE / area_sqmi,
    log_income = log1p(median_incomeE),
    log_density = log1p(pop_density),
    ba_share = bachelorsE / adult_populationE,

title: Building Features: Predicting Philadelphia Commute Times
text:
Part 7: Reflection
The most useful addition is City Hall distance with its squared term, reducing mean fold RMSE by 0.15 minutes from baseline. The curve allows downtown proximity to matter differently near the center and city edge; a single slope misses that variation. Shooting-victim density disappoints most among individual spatial features: I expected neighborhood safety to add context, but its information may overlap with socioeconomic predictors and it measures travel access only indirectly. All safety additions slightly worsen RMSE; these small differences establish no predictive gain here, not a causal absence of safety effects.
For the coefficient reading, β̂ for median household income is 0.009 minutes per $1,000, holding other final-model predictors fixed. For the prediction reading, otherwise identical tracts differing by $10,000 in median income have fitted commute times differing by 0.09 minutes (higher-income minus lower-income). This is an adjusted association between tract averages, not an individual or causal income effect.
Geographic error remains: West (west of 75.19 W) has the largest final mean absolute held-out error among the descriptive sectors. I would next measure jobs reachable within a fixed travel-time budget and historical transit frequency. Census LEHD Origin–Destination Employment Statistics and archived SEPTA GTFS schedules could represent destinations, transfers, and service availability more directly than safety records or straight-line downtown distance. Matching those inputs to 2023 or earlier remains essential.
Finally, the uncertainty plot rises, but the rank correlation of 0.17 is weak and substantial errors remain at moderate CVs. The median approximate outcome standard error is 7.01 minutes; its size emphasizes uncertainty without identifying its share of model error. The ratio approximation omits covariance, and the five-year ACS spans changing commuting conditions. Reusing folds to choose features can make the final improvement optimistic; independent spatial validation is needed before operational use.

title: Assignment 2: Who Do We Know the Least About?
text:
The question
Every number the American Community Survey publishes is an estimate drawn from a sample, not a count. That means every number comes with a margin of error — a statement about how wrong it might be.
Most people ignore it. In this assignment, you won’t.
In this analysis, I look at the median age across counties in Florida, and ask which communities we measure most and least reliably.

section: How big is the margin of error?
text:
How big is the margin of error?
A margin of error of 3,000 means something very different for an estimate of 20,000 than for an estimate of 200,000. To compare across places, we need it as a percentage.

county_data <- county_data %>%
  mutate(moe_pct = moe / estimate * 100)

Now sort to see which counties are measured least reliably.

  arrange(desc(moe_pct)) %>%

Is the margin of error bigger in small places?
To answer this we need population and our variable side by side, in the same row. That means a wide pull.

  geography = "county",
  variables = c(myvar = my_variable,
                pop   = "B01003_001"),
  state = my_state,
  year = 2023,
  survey = "acs5",
  output = "wide"
)

title: Assignment 2: Who Do We Know the Least About?
text:
What this means for policy
[Your 200–250 word reflection goes here.]

In Florida, the communities we know the least about are small, rural counties such as Lafayette County and Liberty County. In our analysis, Lafayette County had the highest relative margin of error at 6.22%, while Liberty County, Florida have the margin of error at 5.37%. This two counties also fell into the moderate confidence category, with an average population of just 7,842.
This uncertainty stems directly from how the American Community Survey (ACS) operates. Because the ACS collects data from a sample of households rather than conducting a full census count, smaller populations naturally yield smaller sample sizes. With fewer completed responses, individual sample variations will lead to higher random variations on a bigger impact, driving up the margin of error percentage relative to the estimate.
If a state agency allocated funding based on median ages, like distributing senior services grants. Treating every county’s estimate as equally certain means that the rural residents would suffer most. In small counties, less sample calculated median age. If Lafayette County’s median age were underestimated due to sampling error and there is more outliner, state algorithms might misclassify it as a younger community and withhold essential funding for senior centers, elder healthcare, and specialized transit. Meanwhile, large urban counties like Miami-Dade have massive sample sizes, negligible relative error, and stable funding streams. Relying uncritically on ACS estimates without accounting for margin of error disproportionately harms vulnerable, small-town communities by compounding statistical uncertainty with financial deprivation.

title: Assignment 3: Verify the Claim - Poverty Change in Philadelphia
text:
Part 1 — Reconstruct
I use B17001_002, the number of people whose income in the past 12 months was below the poverty level, divided by B17001_001, the population for whom poverty status is determined. The denominator is the population covered by this poverty table, rather than the entire population from a separate table. I use the same variables in both periods so that the rates measure the same thing. The Week 3 notes identify B17001_002 as a poverty count; I adapt the practice script’s moe_prop() calculation to this table. The E columns contain estimates and the M columns contain their margins of error.
I request survey = "acs5" with year = 2010 and year = 2017, which represent 2006–2010 and 2013–2017. Five-year estimates are available for tracts, and these are the periods specified in the assignment. The periods do not overlap: they share no survey years. I use the class method that treats their sampling errors as independent. I assume B17001 is an appropriate reconstruction of the article’s poverty measure and that matching tract GEOIDs represent comparable areas. A matching identifier alone does not verify unchanged boundaries. I do not assign neighborhood names to tracts or average tract rates to reconstruct a neighborhood.


Show code
acs_2006_2010 <- get_acs(
  geography = "tract",
  variables = c(
    total_pop = "B17001_001",
    total_poverty = "B17001_002"
  ),
  state = "PA",
  county = "Philadelphia",
  year = 2010,
  survey = "acs5",
  output = "wide"
)

acs_2013_2017 <- get_acs(
  geography = "tract",
  variables = c(
    total_pop = "B17001_001",
    total_poverty = "B17001_002"

title: Assignment 3: Verify the Claim - Poverty Change in Philadelphia
text:
Part 2 — Test

Calculate rates and investigate missing values
I combine the two downloads with a period label, then apply the same calculation to every tract-period row. Multiplying both the proportion and its MOE by 100 expresses the rate as a percentage and the MOE in percentage points. I check the original counts before calculating rates: a zero denominator makes a rate undefined, rather than making it a zero-poverty tract. Missing or invalid inputs remain unavailable.


Show code
poverty_rates <- bind_rows(
  acs_2006_2010 %>% mutate(period = "2006-2010"),
  acs_2013_2017 %>% mutate(period = "2013-2017")
) %>%
  mutate(
    input_status = case_when(
      is.na(total_popE) | is.na(total_povertyE) |
        is.na(total_popM) | is.na(total_povertyM) ~ "Missing count or MOE",
      total_popE == 0 ~ "Zero poverty-universe population",
      total_popE < 0 | total_povertyE < 0 |
        total_povertyE > total_popE |
        total_popM < 0 | total_povertyM < 0 ~ "Invalid count or MOE",
      TRUE ~ "Usable"
    ),
    # NA prevents division by zero while preserving the original counts.
    denominator = if_else(input_status == "Usable", total_popE, NA_real_),
    pov_rate = 100 * total_povertyE / denominator,
    pov_rate_moe = 100 * moe_prop(
      total_povertyE, denominator, total_povertyM, total_popM
    ),
    # CV is undefined for a zero rate; its rate and MOE can still be used.
    cv = if_else(pov_rate > 0,
                 (pov_rate_moe / 1.645) / pov_rate * 100, NA_real_),
    reliability = case_when(
      is.na(pov_rate) | is.na(pov_rate_moe) ~ "Unavailable rate or MOE",
      pov_rate == 0 ~ "CV undefined: zero rate",
      cv < 12   ~ "Reliable",
      cv <= 40  ~ "Somewhat reliable",
      TRUE      ~ "Unreliable"
    )
  )

missing_inputs <- poverty_rates %>%
  filter(input_status != "Usable")

missing_inputs %>%
  select(GEOID, period, total_popE, total_povertyE, input_status) %>%

The input check identifies 15 unusable tract-period rows: 7 in 2006–2010 and 8 in 2013–2017. In these downloads, all have a zero poverty-universe population. This explains their undefined rates; the counts alone do not identify their land use or prove that their total resident population is zero. I retain these rows in the audit and exclude a tract from the change test if either period lacks a usable rate or MOE.


Match tracts and test changes
I join by GEOID, following the Week 4 notes. A full join keeps unmatched identifiers visible. Change is the later rate minus the earlier rate, in percentage points. Following the practice script, I divide each MOE by 1.645 to get its standard error, combine the two standard errors, and multiply by 1.645 for the MOE of the change. A change is detectable at 90% confidence when abs(z) > 1.645, meaning its interval excludes zero. Reliability describes the precision of an individual rate; it is separate from this test of change.


Show code
selected_2010 <- poverty_rates %>%
  filter(period == "2006-2010") %>%
  select(GEOID, pov_rate_2010 = pov_rate, pov_moe_2010 = pov_rate_moe)

selected_2017 <- poverty_rates %>%
  filter(period == "2013-2017") %>%
  select(GEOID, pov_rate_2017 = pov_rate, pov_moe_2017 = pov_rate_moe)

unmatched_2010 <- anti_join(selected_2010, selected_2017, by = "GEOID")
unmatched_2017 <- anti_join(selected_2017, selected_2010, by = "GEOID")

poverty_wide <- full_join(selected_2010, selected_2017, by = "GEOID")

poverty_tested <- poverty_wide %>%
  mutate(
    change = pov_rate_2017 - pov_rate_2010,
    se_1 = pov_moe_2010 / 1.645,
    se_2 = pov_moe_2017 / 1.645,
    se_diff = sqrt(se_1^2 + se_2^2),
    moe_diff = se_diff * 1.645,
    z = if_else(se_diff > 0, change / se_diff, NA_real_),
    significant = abs(z) > 1.645,
    result = case_when(
      is.na(significant) ~ "Not testable",
      significant & change > 0 ~ "Detectable increase",
      significant & change < 0 ~ "Detectable decrease",
      TRUE ~ "No detectable change"
    )
  )


# Create the summary before the inline R expressions use it below.
test_summary <- poverty_tested %>%
  summarize(
    total = n(),
    tested = sum(!is.na(significant)),
    detected = sum(significant, na.rm = TRUE),
    not_detected = sum(!significant, na.rm = TRUE),
    excluded = sum(is.na(significant)),
    increases = sum(result == "Detectable increase"),
    decreases = sum(result == "Detectable decrease"),
    apparent_increases = sum(change > 0, na.rm = TRUE)
  )

change_counts <- poverty_tested %>% count(result, name = "tracts")
change_counts %>%
  gt() %>%
  cols_label(result = "90% change-test result", tracts = "Number of tracts") %>%
  tab_header(
    title = "Poverty-rate change across Philadelphia tracts",
    subtitle = "ACS 2013–2017 minus 2006–2010 | All downloaded GEOIDs"

The dashed line marks zero change. An error bar crossing this line means that the estimated change is not statistically detectable. Bars above zero are estimated increases; those below zero are estimated decreases. The chart keeps both detectable and non-detectable changes so the reader can compare them.


Reliability of the rates
The CV is the rate’s standard error divided by its estimate, multiplied by 100. I use the assignment’s thresholds: below 12% reliable, 12–40% somewhat reliable, and above 40% unreliable. title: Assignment 3: Verify the Claim - Poverty Change in Philadelphia
text:
Part 3 — Adjudicate
Supported: the broader idea that poverty rates increased in some Philadelphia areas is consistent with the tract evidence: 36 tracts have detectable increases. Change is not uniform, however; 27 tracts have detectable decreases. Not supported: interpreting every positive estimate as established worsening would go beyond the evidence. Of 211 positive changes, only 36 pass the 90% test, and 313 testable tracts overall have intervals that include zero. This is a limit on what can be inferred from the estimates, not evidence that the article explicitly claimed every tract worsened or that every non-detectable change is actually zero.
Cannot be determined: the specific claim that Eastwick rose from 12% to 26%, and especially that its increase was the largest among neighborhoods, cannot be established or contradicted by these tract results. The assignment says the article’s neighborhood groupings are unavailable. A neighborhood rate would require the appropriate aggregated counts and their uncertainty, not an average of tract percentages. A tract with an increase above 14 percentage points would not disprove Eastwick’s neighborhood ranking because tracts and neighborhoods are different units. This report also makes no finding about the article title’s racial comparisons: the two variables used here describe poverty for the full poverty universe, without a race breakdown.

title: Assignment 3: Verify the Claim - Poverty Change in Philadelphia
text:
Part 4 — Rewrite
Philadelphia’s poverty changes were uneven between 2006–2010 and 2013–2017. Among 376 census tracts with usable estimates, 36 showed a statistically detectable increase in poverty rates and 27 showed a detectable decrease at 90% confidence. Changes in the other 313 tracts were too uncertain to distinguish from zero. Another 8 tracts could not be compared because their poverty rates were undefined in at least one period. These findings support increases in some parts of the city, but they do not establish Eastwick’s reported rise from 12% to 26% or its ranking among neighborhoods. Checking those claims requires the tract groupings used to define each neighborhood.

title: Assignment: Building Features, Watching What Happens
text:
This is not a competition. There’s no leaderboard and no target RMSE. The goal is to practice the full prediction workflow on a question you choose, and to find out what actually helps. Some features you’re sure will help won’t, and some you add on a whim will. Both are findings.
You’ll:

Choose a tract-level outcome for Philadelphia and check whether it’s reliable enough to model (Weeks 2–3).
Fit a baseline model and cross-validate it (Week 5).
Pull data from Philadelphia’s open data portal through its API and build spatial features: counts, densities, and distances (Week 4, plus one new tool).
Transform variables with logs, squared terms, and categories. Watch the October 9 recorded lecture before Part 5.
Keep a model log the whole way through, and compare where your first and final models go wrong.

Timing. Parts 1–4 use only what we’ve covered through Week 5. You can finish them before the October 9 lecture. Part 5 is new material; the lecture explains it, and the instructions below give you the essentials.
Type the code yourself. The worked examples show the pattern. Your job is to apply it to your outcome and your data choices.








Important1. Don’t drop rows



Every model is cross-validated on the same tracts with the same folds, so the rows in your model log are comparable. If a new variable has missing values, fill them (for example, 0 for a count, or the median with a note) or choose a different variable. Part 0: Setup

library(tidyverse)

library(sf)

Sys.getenv("CENSUS_API_KEY") != ""   # should print TRUE



The cross-validation helper
This function runs 10-fold cross-validation with the same seed every time, so every model in your log is tested on the same folds. You don’t need to change it. Read it once so you know what it does.


Code
ctrl <- trainControl(method = "cv", number = 10)

cv_rmse <- function(formula, data) {
  df <- if (inherits(data, "sf")) st_drop_geometry(data) else data
  vars <- all.vars(formula)
  bad <- vars[sapply(vars, function(v) any(is.na(df[[v]])))]
  if (length(bad) > 0) {
    stop("These variables have NAs: ", paste(bad, collapse = ", "),
         ". Fill them or choose another variable (Rule 1: don't drop rows).")
  }
  set.seed(5080)
  fit <- train(formula, data = df, method = "lm", trControl = ctrl)
  fit$results$RMSE
}




The model log
Every time you fit a new model, add a row. By the end, this table is the story of your assignment.

model_log <- tibble(
  model   = character(),
  added   = character(),
  cv_rmse = numeric(),
  notes   = character()
)

text:
Part 3: Getting data from Philadelphia’s open data portal
Many of the city’s datasets on OpenDataPhilly are served through a Carto SQL API. You send a SQL query in a URL, and it sends back data. Ask for format=GeoJSON and st_read() reads the result directly, just like the Indego feed in Week 4.
The pattern:
https://phl.carto.com/api/v2/sql?format=GeoJSON&q=SELECT ... FROM table_name WHERE ...
Three pieces of SQL are all you need:

SELECT the_geom, column1, column2 chooses which columns come back. Always include the_geom, or you get no geometry.
FROM table_name chooses the dataset.
WHERE ... filters rows. Filter in the query, not in R. Some tables have millions of rows, and pulling everything will be slow or fail.

This helper builds the URL for you. Spaces and symbols in a URL need encoding, and URLencode() handles that.


Code
carto_get <- function(sql) {
  url <- paste0("https://phl.carto.com/api/v2/sql?format=GeoJSON&q=", URLencode(sql))
  st_read(url, quiet = TRUE)
}



Finding a table name
On a dataset’s OpenDataPhilly page, look for the API link. The table name is the word after FROM in the example query. To see what values a column takes before you filter on it, ask for a count in CSV format:


Code
# What kinds of crime are in the incidents table in 2023?

                         FROM incidents_part1_part2
                         WHERE dispatch_date >= '2023-01-01' AND dispatch_date < '2024-01-01'
                         GROUP BY text_general_code ORDER BY n DESC"))
read_csv(url)

Part 4: Building spatial features
Every feature below reuses a Week 4 tool. The worked examples use burglaries and Indego stations; you build the same types from your own layers.

4A: Counting
How many burglaries fall in each tract?


Code
tracts <- tracts %>%
  mutate(n_burglary = lengths(st_intersects(., burglary)))

summary(tracts$n_burglary)


A tract with no burglaries gets 0, not NA, so Rule 1 is safe.


4B: Density: don’t skip this
Raw counts mostly measure tract size. A big tract has more of everything. Normalize by area, by population, or by housing units, depending on what makes sense for the thing you’re counting.


Code
tracts <- tracts %>%
  mutate(
    area_sqmi         = as.numeric(st_area(.)) / 27878400,   # sq ft in a sq mile
    burglary_per_sqmi = n_burglary / area_sqmi,
    burglary_per_1k   = n_burglary / total_popE * 1000
  )








NotePer capita in low-population tracts



If a tract has 40 residents and 3 burglaries, its rate is 75 per 1,000, which is a huge number built on tiny counts. Look at the tracts with the highest per-capita rates before you trust them. This is the Week 3 lesson about small denominators again.




4C: Measuring distance to the nearest thing
How far is each tract from its nearest Indego station? Use the Week 4 pattern: find the nearest feature, then measure to it element by element.


Code
stations <- st_read("https://www.rideindego.com/stations/json/", quiet = TRUE) %>%
  st_transform(st_crs(tracts))

tract_pts <- st_point_on_surface(tracts)   # always inside the tract, unlike a centroid

nearest_idx <- st_nearest_feature(tract_pts, stations)

tracts <- tracts %>%
  mutate(dist_station_mi = as.numeric(
    st_distance(tract_pts, stations[nearest_idx, ], by_element = TRUE)) / 5280)

Sometimes the “thing” is a single location, such as City Hall as a stand-in for the center of the regional economy.


Code

  st_transform(st_crs(tracts))

tracts <- tracts %>%
  mutate(dist_ch_mi = as.numeric(st_distance(tract_pts, city_hall)) / 5280)

text:
Part 5: Transforming features
Watch the October 9 recorded lecture before you start this part. Below is a summary to work from.
So far, every predictor has entered the model as a straight line: each additional unit of X changes predicted Y by the same amount, everywhere. Transformations let the model bend. For prediction, the question is simply does the bend lower CV RMSE? For interpretation, each transformation changes what a coefficient means, so you need to know how to read it.






TipTransform predictors, not your outcome



Keep your outcome y untransformed in this assignment. If you model log(y), your CV RMSE comes out in log units and can’t be compared to the other rows in your log. (Predicting a logged outcome well requires back-transforming, which is an A4 topic.)



5A: Logs, for skewed predictors
Many urban variables are skewed: a few tracts have huge values, and most have small ones. Income, density, and counts are typical. A log compresses the long tail, so a model can use the difference between 1 and 10 as well as the difference between 100 and 1,000.


Code
ggplot(tracts, aes(x = burglary_per_sqmi)) + geom_histogram(bins = 30) + theme_minimal()
ggplot(tracts, aes(x = log1p(burglary_per_sqmi))) + geom_histogram(bins = 30) + theme_minimal()








Warninglog(0) doesn’t exist



log(0) is -Inf, and it will break your model. Counts and densities often include zeros. Use log1p(x), which computes log(x + 1), for anything that can be 0.


Reading the coefficient: when a predictor is logged, a 1% increase in X goes with a change of about β/100 in Y, in Y’s units. With log1p, this reading is approximate for small values of X.


5B: Squared terms, for curves
If your scatterplot bends (rising and then flattening, or falling and then rising), a squared term lets the line curve. Write it with I(), which tells R to do the arithmetic rather than read ^ as formula syntax.


Code
m_sq <- lm(y ~ dist_ch_mi + I(dist_ch_mi^2), data = tracts)
summary(m_sq)


Reading the coefficient: you can’t read either coefficient alone anymore. The effect of X depends on where you are along X. A positive linear term with a negative squared term means Y rises with X and then levels off or turns down. Plot the fitted curve to see it:


Code
ggplot(tracts, aes(x = dist_ch_mi, y = y)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.4) +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", formula = y ~ x + I(x^2), se = FALSE, color = "red") +
  theme_minimal()




5C: Categorical variables
Sometimes a number works better as groups, either because the relationship isn’t smooth or because the categories are meaningful. You can make categories from any variable with case_when() or cut(), and then make sure R treats them as a factor.


Code
tracts <- tracts %>%
  mutate(
    ring = case_when(
      dist_ch_mi < 2 ~ "Core",
      dist_ch_mi < 5 ~ "Inner",
      TRUE           ~ "Outer"
    ),
    ring = factor(ring, levels = c("Core", "Inner", "Outer"))
  )

tracts %>% st_drop_geometry() %>% count(ring)

m_cat <- lm(y ~ ring, data = tracts)
summary(m_cat)


Reading the coefficients: R turns a factor with k categories into k − 1 dummy variables. The category left out is the reference level (here, “Core,” the first level). Each coefficient is the difference from the reference: ringOuter is how much higher or lower predicted Y is in outer tracts compared to core tracts, holding everything else in the model constant. To change the reference, use relevel(ring, ref = "Outer").






NoteCheck your group sizes



If a category has only a handful of tracts, its coefficient is unstable, and in cross-validation some folds may not contain it at all. Aim for at least 20 tracts per category.

    no_2015_match = sum(is.na(___))
  )

Now look at which tracts failed to match:

# 2023 tracts with no 2015 partner
philly_tracts %>%
  st_drop_geometry() %>%
  filter(is.na(med_inc_15E)) %>%
  select(GEOID, NAME) %>%
  head(10)

# 2015 tracts with no 2023 partner: anti_join keeps rows with NO match

  anti_join(st_drop_geometry(philly_tracts), by = "GEOID") %>%

Some NAs aren’t boundary changes. A tract can match but have NA income because the Census suppressed the estimate. How would you tell the two kinds of NA apart?

title: Week 4 Lab: Who Does Indego Reach?
text:
Part 2: Bring in the stations
Indego publishes live station locations as GeoJSON. st_read() reads it directly from the URL.

stations <- st_read("https://www.rideindego.com/stations/json/", quiet = TRUE)

nrow(stations)
glimpse(stations)

Now check the CRS of both layers.

st_crs(philly_tracts)$epsg
st_crs(___)$epsg

Predict before you run: The two numbers are different. What will happen if you try to join them?

st_join(stations, philly_tracts)

That error is sf protecting you. Fix it by translating both layers into Pennsylvania South State Plane, EPSG 2272.






WarningLabel or translation?



st_set_crs() writes a label when the CRS is missing. st_transform() converts coordinates into a different CRS. Both layers here already have a CRS. Which function do you need?



philly_tracts <- philly_tracts %>% ___(crs = 2272)
stations      <- stations %>% ___(crs = 2272)

st_crs(philly_tracts)$units   # what units are we in now?

Write down the units. Every number you type from now on is in these units.

title: Week 4 Lab: Who Does Indego Reach?
text:
Part 3: Join by where
In Part 1b, the join failed because it matched on a label (GEOID), and the label changed. st_join() matches on location instead: a row is matched to whatever it sits on top of. Stations don’t have a GEOID column, and they don’t need one.
Every station gets its tract’s attributes:

stations_with_tract <- st_join(stations, philly_tracts)

stations_with_tract %>%
  st_drop_geometry() %>%
  select(name, GEOID, med_incE, reliability) %>%
  head()

Now go the other way and count stations per tract. The first route is the Week 2 collapse pattern:

station_counts <- stations_with_tract %>%
  st_drop_geometry() %>%
  ___(GEOID)

The second route counts directly:

philly_tracts <- philly_tracts %>%
  mutate(n_stations = lengths(st_intersects(., stations)))


Check your work

sum(philly_tracts$n_stations)
nrow(stations)

These probably don’t match. Discuss as a team: Why not? Find at least one station that explains the gap.
Hints: Look for stations where GEOID is NA in stations_with_tract. For double counts, look for stations that intersect more than one tract: which(lengths(st_intersects(stations, philly_tracts)) > 1).

Part 4: How far is the nearest station?
st_distance() returns a matrix, not a column. Look at its shape first:

centroids <- st_centroid(st_geometry(philly_tracts))

dim(st_distance(centroids, stations))

Instead, find the nearest station for each tract, then measure only that one distance:

nearest_idx <- st_nearest_feature(centroids, ___)

philly_tracts <- philly_tracts %>%
  mutate(
    dist_ft = as.numeric(
      st_distance(centroids, stations[nearest_idx, ], by_element = ___)
    ),
    dist_mi = dist_ft / ___
  )

summary(philly_tracts$dist_mi)

section: Part 5: Buffers, filters, and cutting the dough
text:
Part 5: Buffers, filters, and cutting the dough
Build a half-mile zone around every station and merge the circles into one shape. Remember your units.

station_zone <- stations %>%
  st_buffer(dist = ___) %>%
  st_union()

Pick whole cookies: which tracts don’t touch the zone at all?

outside_zone <- philly_tracts %>%
  st_filter(station_zone, .predicate = ___)

nrow(outside_zone)

Cut the dough: what share of each tract’s area falls inside the zone?

philly_tracts <- philly_tracts %>%
  mutate(tract_area = as.numeric(st_area(.)))

covered <- philly_tracts %>%
  st_intersection(station_zone) %>%
  mutate(covered_area = as.numeric(st_area(.))) %>%
  st_drop_geometry() %>%
  select(GEOID, covered_area)

philly_tracts <- philly_tracts %>%
  left_join(covered, by = "GEOID") %>%
  mutate(pct_covered = replace_na(covered_area / tract_area, 0) * 100)

Notice: that last step is the left_join() from Part 1b. It’s a join by what (GEOID), used to bring a join-by-where result back into the table. The two kinds of join work together.

Part 0: Setup and a fair comparison


Show code
library(tidyverse)
library(tidycensus)
library(sf)

options(tigris_use_cache = TRUE)
theme_set(theme_minimal())
model_log <- tibble(model = character(), added = character(),
                    cv_rmse = numeric(), notes = character())


I assign folds once after defining the shared sample. Every candidate uses the same tracts, fold assignments, and outcome units. This makes the RMSE comparisons fair, though random tract folds test prediction for held-out tracts in Philadelphia rather than transfer to a new city.


Show code
cv_rmse <- function(formula, data, fold_id) {
  stopifnot(length(fold_id) == nrow(data), !anyNA(fold_id))
  predictions <- rep(NA_real_, nrow(data))
  for (k in sort(unique(fold_id))) {
    train_rows <- fold_id != k
    test_rows <- fold_id == k
    fit <- lm(formula, data = data[train_rows, , drop = FALSE],
              na.action = na.fail)
    predictions[test_rows] <- predict(fit, newdata = data[test_rows, , drop = FALSE])
  }
  if (any(!is.finite(predictions))) stop("CV produced missing or non-finite predictions.")
  sqrt(mean((data$y - predictions)^2))
}

section: Part 5: Transformations, distance rings, and planning-district effects
text:
Part 5: Transformations, distance rings, and planning-district effects
I inspect distributions and relationships before choosing transformations. log1p() accommodates zero burglary densities. A squared City Hall distance lets the commute-time relationship curve; I interpret the linear and squared coefficients together and check whether the calculated turning point is inside the observed range. The outcome stays in minutes, so all RMSE values remain comparable.


Show code
ggplot(model_data, aes(x = burglary_per_sqmi)) + geom_histogram(bins = 30) +
  labs(x = "Residential burglaries per square mile")









Show code
ggplot(model_data, aes(x = dist_ch_mi, y = y)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.4) +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", formula = y ~ x + I(x^2), se = FALSE) +
  labs(x = "Distance from City Hall (miles)", y = "Mean commute time (minutes)")










5A. Log feature


Show code
tracts$log_burglary <- log1p(tracts$burglary_per_sqmi)
model_data <- tracts %>% st_drop_geometry()
f_log <- update(f1, . ~ . + log_burglary)
model_log <- model_log %>% add_row(
  model = "m8", added = "Log1p burglary density",
  cv_rmse = cv_rmse(f_log, model_data, folds), notes = "Zero-safe log transformation"
)




5B. Squared distance and the turning point
The coefficient on dist_ch_mi alone is not the effect of distance in this model. The fitted change per additional mile at distance x is β₁ + 2β₂x. The turning point is −β₁/(2β₂); I check it against observed tract distances before describing a bend as occurring in Philadelphia’s data.


Show code
f_sq <- update(f1, . ~ . + dist_ch_mi + I(dist_ch_mi^2))
m_sq <- lm(f_sq, data = model_data)
b1 <- unname(coef(m_sq)["dist_ch_mi"])
b2 <- unname(coef(m_sq)["I(dist_ch_mi^2)"])
turning_point <- if (is.finite(b2) && b2 != 0) -b1 / (2 * b2) else NA_real_
distance_range <- range(model_data$dist_ch_mi, na.rm = TRUE)
turning_inside <- is.finite(turning_point) &&
  turning_point >= distance_range[1] && turning_point <= distance_range[2]
tibble(linear_coefficient = b1, squared_coefficient = b2,
       turning_point_miles = turning_point,
       observed_min = distance_range[1], observed_max = distance_range[2],
       turning_point_inside_range = turning_inside)

Show code

  model = "m9", added = "Squared City Hall distance",
  cv_rmse = cv_rmse(f_sq, model_data, folds),

I plot fitted values over the observed distance range while holding the other baseline predictors at their medians. This shows the model’s curve without extrapolating beyond the tracts in the sample.

The estimated bend is within the observed range, though it remains an association rather than a causal effect.

title: Assignment 4: Building Features, Watching What Happens
text:
This is not a competition. There’s no leaderboard and no target RMSE. The goal is to practice the full prediction workflow on a question you choose, and to find out what actually helps. Some features you’re sure will help won’t, and some you add on a whim will. Both are findings.
You’ll:

Choose a tract-level outcome for Philadelphia and check whether it’s reliable enough to model (Weeks 2–3).
Fit a baseline model and cross-validate it (Week 5).
Pull data from Philadelphia’s open data portal through its API and build spatial features: counts, densities, and distances (Week 4, plus one new tool).
Transform variables with logs, squared terms, and categories. Watch the October 9 recorded lecture before Part 5.
Keep a model log the whole way through, and compare where your first and final models go wrong.

Timing. Parts 1–4 use only what we’ve covered through Week 5. You can finish them before the October 9 lecture. Part 5 is new material; the lecture explains it, and the instructions below give you the essentials.
Type the code yourself. The worked examples show the pattern. Your job is to apply it to your outcome and your data choices.








Important1. Don’t drop rows



Every model is cross-validated on the same tracts with the same folds, so the rows in your model log are comparable. If a new variable has missing values, fill them (for example, 0 for a count, or the median with a note) or choose a different variable. The cv_rmse() helper below will stop and tell you if you break this rule.


Your outcome comes from the 2019–2023 ACS. Pull open data from 2023 or earlier (2021–2023 is ideal). Using 2025 data to predict a 2023 outcome uses information from the future, which a real prediction model would never have.



Don’t use any variable that’s built from your outcome or measures the same thing another way. Ask yourself: would an agency trying to predict this outcome for a tract have this variable? If the answer is “only because it’s basically the outcome,” leave it out.

section: Part 3: Getting data from Philadelphia’s open data portal
text:
Part 3: Getting data from Philadelphia’s open data portal
Many of the city’s datasets on OpenDataPhilly are served through a Carto SQL API. You send a SQL query in a URL, and it sends back data. Ask for format=GeoJSON and st_read() reads the result directly, just like the Indego feed in Week 4.
The pattern:
https://phl.carto.com/api/v2/sql?format=GeoJSON&q=SELECT ... FROM table_name WHERE ...
Three pieces of SQL are all you need:

SELECT the_geom, column1, column2 chooses which columns come back. Always include the_geom, or you get no geometry.
FROM table_name chooses the dataset.

title: Assignment 4: Building Features, Watching What Happens
text:
Part 4: Building spatial features
Every feature below reuses a Week 4 tool. The worked examples use burglaries and Indego stations; you build the same types from your own layers.

4A: Counting
How many burglaries fall in each tract?


Code
tracts <- tracts %>%
  mutate(n_burglary = lengths(st_intersects(., burglary)))

summary(tracts$n_burglary)


   Min. 1st Qu.  Median    Mean 3rd Qu.    Max. 
  0.000   4.000   7.000   9.458  13.000  48.000 


A tract with no burglaries gets 0, not NA, so Rule 1 is safe.


4B: Density: don’t skip this
Raw counts mostly measure tract size. A big tract has more of everything. Normalize by area, by population, or by housing units, depending on what makes sense for the thing you’re counting.


Code
tracts <- tracts %>%
  mutate(
    area_sqmi         = as.numeric(st_area(.)) / 27878400,   # sq ft in a sq mile
    burglary_per_sqmi = n_burglary / area_sqmi,
    burglary_per_1k   = n_burglary / total_popE * 1000
  )








NotePer capita in low-population tracts



If a tract has 40 residents and 3 burglaries, its rate is 75 per 1,000, which is a huge number built on tiny counts. Look at the tracts with the highest per-capita rates before you trust them. This is the Week 3 lesson about small denominators again.




4C: Measuring distance to the nearest thing
How far is each tract from its nearest Indego station? Use the Week 4 pattern: find the nearest feature, then measure to it element by element.


Code
stations <- st_read("https://www.rideindego.com/stations/json/", quiet = TRUE) %>%
  st_transform(st_crs(tracts))

tract_pts <- st_point_on_surface(tracts)   # always inside the tract, unlike a centroid

nearest_idx <- st_nearest_feature(tract_pts, stations)

tracts <- tracts %>%
  mutate(dist_station_mi = as.numeric(
    st_distance(tract_pts, stations[nearest_idx, ], by_element = TRUE)) / 5280)




4D: Measuring distance to one place
Sometimes the “thing” is a single location, such as City Hall as a stand-in for the center of the regional economy.


Code
city_hall <- st_sfc(st_point(c(-75.1636, 39.9526)), crs = 4326) %>%
  st_transform(st_crs(tracts))

tracts <- tracts %>%
  mutate(dist_ch_mi = as.numeric(st_distance(tract_pts, city_hall)) / 5280)




4E: Your turn
Build at least three spatial features from your own layers, and use at least two types (count, density, nearest distance, distance to a place). After each one, fit a model, cross-validate it, and log it.


Code
# Feature 1: count burglaries in each tract
tracts <- tracts %>% mutate(n_burglary = lengths(st_intersects(., layer1)))
f2 <- update(f1, . ~ . + n_burglary)
m2 <- lm(f2, data = tracts)
model_log <- model_log %>%
  add_row(model = "m2", added = "burglary count", cv_rmse = cv_rmse(f2, tracts),
          notes = "Adds 2023 residential burglary count")

# Feature 2: normalize count by tract area
tracts <- tracts %>% mutate(area_sqmi = as.numeric(st_area(.)) / 27878400,
                            burglary_per_sqmi = n_burglary / area_sqmi)
f3 <- update(f2, . ~ . + burglary_per_sqmi)
m3 <- lm(f3, data = tracts)
model_log <- model_log %>%
  add_row(model = "m3", added = "burglaries per square mile", cv_rmse = cv_rmse(f3, tracts),
          notes = "Adds area-normalized 2023 burglary count")

# Feature 3: distance to nearest Indego station
tract_pts <- st_point_on_surface(tracts)
nearest_station_idx <- st_nearest_feature(tract_pts, layer2)
tracts <- tracts %>% mutate(dist_station_mi = as.numeric(
  st_distance(tract_pts, layer2[nearest_station_idx, ], by_element = TRUE)) / 5280)
f4 <- update(f3, . ~ . + dist_station_mi)
m4 <- lm(f4, data = tracts)
model_log <- model_log %>%
  add_row(model = "m4", added = "distance to nearest Indego station", cv_rmse = cv_rmse(f4, tracts),
          notes = "Adds nearest-station distance in miles")
model_log

2 m2    burglary count                        5.14 Adds 2023 residential burgla…
3 m3    burglaries per square mile            5.16 Adds area-normalized 2023 bu…
4 m4    distance to nearest Indego station    5.17 Adds nearest-station distanc…


Answer: Which spatial feature helped most? Did any feature you expected to help do nothing, or make CV RMSE worse? Why might that be?
Your answer:
Among the spatial additions, burglary count has the lowest CV RMSE (5.14 minutes). Compared with the baseline, the spatial model(s) that made CV RMSE worse are m2, m3, m4. Burglary may add only an indirect signal about commuting, and Indego distance does not measure SEPTA service or job destinations, so either could add little or even increase CV error.

title: Assignment 4: Building Features, Watching What Happens
text:
Part 5: Transforming features
Watch the October 9 recorded lecture before you start this part. Below is a summary to work from.
So far, every predictor has entered the model as a straight line: each additional unit of X changes predicted Y by the same amount, everywhere. Transformations let the model bend. For prediction, the question is simply does the bend lower CV RMSE? For interpretation, each transformation changes what a coefficient means, so you need to know how to read it.






TipTransform predictors, not your outcome



Keep your outcome y untransformed in this assignment. If you model log(y), your CV RMSE comes out in log units and can’t be compared to the other rows in your log. (Predicting a logged outcome well requires back-transforming, which is an A4 topic.)



5A: Logs, for skewed predictors
Many urban variables are skewed: a few tracts have huge values, and most have small ones. Income, density, and counts are typical. A log compresses the long tail, so a model can use the difference between 1 and 10 as well as the difference between 100 and 1,000.


Code
ggplot(tracts, aes(x = burglary_per_sqmi)) + geom_histogram(bins = 30) + theme_minimal()









Code
ggplot(tracts, aes(x = log1p(burglary_per_sqmi))) + geom_histogram(bins = 30) + theme_minimal()















Warninglog(0) doesn’t exist



log(0) is -Inf, and it will break your model. Counts and densities often include zeros. Use log1p(x), which computes log(x + 1), for anything that can be 0.


Reading the coefficient: when a predictor is logged, a 1% increase in X goes with a change of about β/100 in Y, in Y’s units. With log1p, this reading is approximate for small values of X.


5B: Squared terms, for curves
If your scatterplot bends (rising and then flattening, or falling and then rising), a squared term lets the line curve. Write it with I(), which tells R to do the arithmetic rather than read ^ as formula syntax.


Code
m_sq <- lm(y ~ dist_ch_mi + I(dist_ch_mi^2), data = tracts)
summary(m_sq)



Call:
lm(formula = y ~ dist_ch_mi + I(dist_ch_mi^2), data = tracts)

Residuals:

-18.5194  -3.0884  -0.0491   2.9256  16.3693 

Coefficients:

(Intercept)     25.87577    0.69995  36.968  < 2e-16 ***
dist_ch_mi       2.10433    0.25419   8.279 2.19e-15 ***
I(dist_ch_mi^2) -0.12422    0.01908  -6.511 2.39e-10 ***
---

Multiple R-squared:  0.1911,    Adjusted R-squared:  0.1868 
F-statistic: 44.54 on 2 and 377 DF,  p-value: < 2.2e-16


Reading the coefficient: you can’t read either coefficient alone anymore. The effect of X depends on where you are along X. A positive linear term with a negative squared term means Y rises with X and then levels off or turns down. Plot the fitted curve to see it:


Code
ggplot(tracts, aes(x = dist_ch_mi, y = y)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.4) +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", formula = y ~ x + I(x^2), se = FALSE, color = "red") +
  theme_minimal()











5C: Categorical variables
Sometimes a number works better as groups, either because the relationship isn’t smooth or because the categories are meaningful. You can make categories from any variable with case_when() or cut(), and then make sure R treats them as a factor.


Code
tracts <- tracts %>%
  mutate(
    ring = case_when(
      dist_ch_mi < 2 ~ "Core",
      dist_ch_mi < 5 ~ "Inner",
      TRUE           ~ "Outer"
    ),
    ring = factor(ring, levels = c("Core", "Inner", "Outer"))
  )

tracts %>% st_drop_geometry() %>% count(ring)


   ring   n
1  Core  79
2 Inner 134
3 Outer 167


Code
m_cat <- lm(y ~ ring, data = tracts)
summary(m_cat)



Call:
lm(formula = y ~ ring, data = tracts)

Residuals:
     Min       1Q   Median       3Q      Max 
-17.5146  -3.2886  -0.1537   3.1284  17.1430 

Coefficients:
            Estimate Std. Error t value Pr(>|t|)    
(Intercept)  27.5537     0.5699  48.349  < 2e-16 ***
ringInner     4.3575     0.7185   6.065 3.21e-09 ***
ringOuter     6.4529     0.6917   9.329  < 2e-16 ***
---
Signif. codes:  0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 '.' 0.1 ' ' 1

Residual standard error: 5.065 on 377 degrees of freedom
Multiple R-squared:  0.1876,    Adjusted R-squared:  0.1833 
F-statistic: 43.52 on 2 and 377 DF,  p-value: < 2.2e-16


Reading the coefficients: R turns a factor with k categories into k − 1 dummy variables. The category left out is the reference level (here, “Core,” the first level). Each coefficient is the difference from the reference: ringOuter is how much higher or lower predicted Y is in outer tracts compared to core tracts, holding everything else in the model constant. To change the reference, use relevel(ring, ref = "Outer").






NoteCheck your group sizes



If a category has only a handful of tracts, its coefficient is unstable, and in cross-validation some folds may not contain it at all. Aim for at least 20 tracts per category.




5D: Your turn
Try at least one of each: a log, a squared term, and a categorical variable. Choose which variables to transform based on your plots, not at random. Log each model.

# Log transform skewed median household income
tracts <- tracts %>% mutate(log_income = log1p(median_incomeE))
f_log <- update(f4, . ~ . - median_incomeE + log_income)
model_log <- model_log %>%
  add_row(model = "m5", added = "log of median household income",
          cv_rmse = cv_rmse(f_log, tracts), notes = "Replaces raw income with log1p(income)")

# Allow the station-distance relationship to curve
f_sq <- update(f4, . ~ . + I(dist_station_mi^2))
model_log <- model_log %>%
  add_row(model = "m6", added = "squared distance to Indego station",
          cv_rmse = cv_rmse(f_sq, tracts), notes = "Tests a curved station-distance relationship")

# Compare income quartiles as categories
tracts <- tracts %>% mutate(income_group = factor(dplyr::ntile(median_incomeE, 4),
  levels = 1:4, labels = c("Q1_lowest", "Q2", "Q3", "Q4_highest")))
f_cat <- update(f4, . ~ . - median_incomeE + income_group)
m_cat <- lm(f_cat, data = tracts)
model_log <- model_log %>%
  add_row(model = "m7", added = "income quartile factor",
          cv_rmse = cv_rmse(f_cat, tracts), notes = "Replaces linear income with four income groups")
model_log

Answer: Which transformation helped most? For your categorical variable, write one sentence reading one of its coefficients correctly, naming the reference level.
Your answer:
The transformation with the lowest CV RMSE is squared distance to Indego station (5.12 minutes). In the categorical model, Q1_lowest is the reference group: holding the other predictors in that model constant, Q4_highest tracts are predicted to have 1.5 minutes shorter mean commutes than Q1_lowest tracts.

text:
Part 7: Reflection (about 300 words)
Answer in prose, drawing on your model log (incorporate our words of the day for bonus points. just kidding):

What helped, and what didn’t? Name the feature that lowered CV RMSE the most and the one that disappointed you most. Offer a reason for each.
Read one coefficient twice. Choose a variable in your final model. Give its β̂ reading and its ŷ reading in one sentence each.
What’s still missing? Look at your final residual map. Name one thing about those places you’d want to measure next, and where you might get the data.
How much of the remaining error might be uncertainty or statistical noise? Use your last plot.

Your answer:
The best tested addition is squared distance to Indego station; the weakest is log of median household income. Their CV RMSEs are 5.12 and 5.18 minutes; CV error on unseen tracts is the basis for choosing features. In the final model, a one-percentage-point increase in bachelor’s-or-higher share changes predicted commute time by -0.07 minutes, holding other predictors constant. For tract GEOID 42101034701, with bachelor’s share closest to the sample median, the final model predicts 34.51 minutes.
The residual map and the feature comparisons suggest where the model needs more information. A useful next measure would be transit travel time and service frequency to job centers, using SEPTA schedules and Census LEHD/LODES job locations. Burglary is only an indirect measure of neighborhood context, and station distance does not capture routes, transfers, or frequency, so those spatial features can help little even when the underlying idea matters. The correlation between ACS outcome CV and absolute final residual is 0.28. A positive association means larger misses tend to occur where the ACS outcome is less reliable; it would suggest uncertainty contributes to the error, but it would not establish that uncertainty explains all of it. I would also compare the residual map with the reliability plot, since places with reliable ACS estimates can still have large prediction errors when the model omits important local conditions. The log-income model tests whether income has diminishing returns, the squared-distance model allows the station relationship to bend, and the income-group model allows step changes between quartiles. Whichever gives the smallest held-out error earns its place as a predictive feature, even if its coefficient is not statistically significant. These comparisons describe predictive association across tracts, not the causal effect of changing income, education, or infrastructure.

This is not a competition. There’s no leaderboard and no target RMSE. The goal is to practice the full prediction workflow on a question you choose, and to find out what actually helps. Some features you’re sure will help won’t, and some you add on a whim will. Both are findings.
You’ll:

Choose a tract-level outcome for Philadelphia and check whether it’s reliable enough to model (Weeks 2–3).
Fit a baseline model and cross-validate it (Week 5).
Pull data from Philadelphia’s open data portal through its API and build spatial features: counts, densities, and distances (Week 4, plus one new tool).
Transform variables with logs, squared terms, and categories. Watch the October 9 recorded lecture before Part 5.
Keep a model log the whole way through, and compare where your first and final models go wrong.

Timing. Parts 1–4 use only what we’ve covered through Week 5. You can finish them before the October 9 lecture. Part 5 is new material; the lecture explains it, and the instructions below give you the essentials.
Type the code yourself. The worked examples show the pattern. Your job is to apply it to your outcome and your data choices.








Important1. Don’t drop rows



Every model is cross-validated on the same tracts with the same folds, so the rows in your model log are comparable. If a new variable has missing values, fill them (for example, 0 for a count, or the median with a note) or choose a different variable. The cv_rmse() helper below will stop and tell you if you break this rule.


Your outcome comes from the 2019–2023 ACS. Pull open data from 2023 or earlier (2021–2023 is ideal). Using 2025 data to predict a 2023 outcome uses information from the future, which a real prediction model would never have.



Don’t use any variable that’s built from your outcome or measures the same thing another way. Ask yourself: would an agency trying to predict this outcome for a tract have this variable? If the answer is “only because it’s basically the outcome,” leave it out.

text:
Part 0: Setup


Code
library(tidyverse)
library(tidycensus)
library(sf)
library(caret)

Sys.getenv("CENSUS_API_KEY") != ""   # should print TRUE


[1] TRUE



The cross-validation helper
This function runs 10-fold cross-validation with the same seed every time, so every model in your log is tested on the same folds. You don’t need to change it. Read it once so you know what it does.


Code
ctrl <- trainControl(method = "cv", number = 10)

cv_rmse <- function(formula, data) {
  df <- if (inherits(data, "sf")) st_drop_geometry(data) else data
  vars <- all.vars(formula)
  bad <- vars[sapply(vars, function(v) any(is.na(df[[v]])))]
  if (length(bad) > 0) {
    stop("These variables have NAs: ", paste(bad, collapse = ", "),
         ". Fill them or choose another variable (Rule 1: don't drop rows).")
  }
  set.seed(5080)
  fit <- train(formula, data = df, method = "lm", trControl = ctrl)
  fit$results$RMSE
}

  mutate(across(where(is.numeric) & matches("[EM]$"), ~ if_else(.x < 0, NA_real_, .x)),
    area_sqmi = as.numeric(units::set_units(st_area(.), "mi^2")),
    commute_denom = if_else(commutersE > 0, commutersE, NA_real_),
    y = travel_minutesE / commute_denom,
    y_moe = moe_ratio(num = travel_minutesE, denom = commute_denom,
                     moe_num = travel_minutesM, moe_denom = commutersM),
    y_cv = if_else(y > 0, (y_moe / 1.645) / y * 100, NA_real_),
    income_k = median_incomeE / 1000,
    ba_share = 100 * (bachelorsE + mastersE + professionalE + doctorateE) /
      if_else(pop_25_plusE > 0, pop_25_plusE, NA_real_),
    renter_share = 100 * renter_occupiedE /
      if_else(occupied_unitsE > 0, occupied_unitsE, NA_real_),
    pop_density_k = total_popE / area_sqmi / 1000,
    reliability = case_when(!is.finite(y_cv) ~ "Unavailable",
      y_cv < 12 ~ "High", y_cv <= 40 ~ "Moderate", TRUE ~ "Low"))

Part 3: Philadelphia open data
I use 2023 residential burglaries and shooting-victim records. Burglary measures reported property crime near residences; victim locations describe exposure to serious violence. Safety conditions might correlate with travel choices and neighborhood disinvestment after the ACS controls, but this is a hypothesis to test. Neither layer directly measures transit access, and reporting/geocoding differences limit interpretation. A shooting-victim record is a victim, not necessarily a unique shooting incident.


Show code
carto_get <- function(sql) {
  url <- paste0("https://phl.carto.com/api/v2/sql?format=GeoJSON&q=",
                 URLencode(sql, reserved = TRUE))
  st_read(url, quiet = TRUE)
}
burglary_raw <- cached_data("burglary_2023", function() carto_get(
  "SELECT the_geom, text_general_code, dispatch_date
   FROM incidents_part1_part2
   WHERE dispatch_date >= '2023-01-01' AND dispatch_date < '2024-01-01'
     AND text_general_code = 'Burglary Residential'"))

  "SELECT the_geom, date_ FROM shootings
   WHERE date_ >= '2023-01-01' AND date_ < '2024-01-01'"))

  usable <- !st_is_empty(x) & (st_is_valid(x) %in% TRUE)

    downloaded = nrow(x), missing_or_invalid = sum(!usable),

Part 6: Final model

Combine useful features, then compare
Starting with the baseline, I consider the better count/raw-density/log-density version of burglary, victim density, nearest-victim distance, and the better linear/quadratic/categorical City Hall measure, in that order. I attempt a feature only when its individual candidate beats baseline and retain it in the combination only if it improves the current score. Every attempted combination is logged. This is a small search, not exhaustive subset selection. I choose the lowest RMSE among all evaluated candidates; ties favor the earlier specification.


Show code
best_id <- function(ids) {
  z <- model_log %>% filter(model %in% ids)
  z$model[which.min(z$cv_rmse)]

baseline_terms <- attr(terms(f1), "term.labels")
for (i in seq_along(candidate_groups)) {
  id <- best_id(candidate_groups[[i]])
  if (model_log$cv_rmse[match(id, model_log$model)] >= model_log$cv_rmse[1]) next
  extra_terms <- setdiff(attr(terms(formulas[[id]]), "term.labels"), baseline_terms)
  combined <- reformulate(unique(c(attr(terms(formulas[[current_id]]), "term.labels"),
                                    extra_terms)), response = "y")
  combined_id <- paste0("combine", i)
  log_model(combined_id, combined, paste("Add", model_log$added[match(id, model_log$model)]),
            current_id, "Retain only if CV RMSE decreases")
  if (tail(model_log$improvement, 1) > 0) current_id <- combined_id
}

title: Building Features: Predicting Philadelphia Commute Times
text:
Part 7: Reflection
The most useful addition is City Hall distance with its squared term, reducing mean fold RMSE by 0.15 minutes from baseline. The curve allows downtown proximity to matter differently near the center and city edge; a single slope misses that variation. Shooting-victim density disappoints most among individual spatial features: I expected neighborhood safety to add context, but its information may overlap with socioeconomic predictors and it measures travel access only indirectly. All safety additions slightly worsen RMSE; these small differences establish no predictive gain here, not a causal absence of safety effects.
For the coefficient reading, β̂ for median household income is 0.009 minutes per $1,000, holding other final-model predictors fixed. For the prediction reading, otherwise identical tracts differing by $10,000 in median income have fitted commute times differing by 0.09 minutes (higher-income minus lower-income). This is an adjusted association between tract averages, not an individual or causal income effect.
Geographic error remains: West (west of 75.19 W) has the largest final mean absolute held-out error among the descriptive sectors. I would next measure jobs reachable within a fixed travel-time budget and historical transit frequency. Census LEHD Origin–Destination Employment Statistics and archived SEPTA GTFS schedules could represent destinations, transfers, and service availability more directly than safety records or straight-line downtown distance. Matching those inputs to 2023 or earlier remains essential.
Finally, the uncertainty plot rises, but the rank correlation of 0.17 is weak and substantial errors remain at moderate CVs. The median approximate outcome standard error is 7.01 minutes; its size emphasizes uncertainty without identifying its share of model error. The ratio approximation omits covariance, and the five-year ACS spans changing commuting conditions. Reusing folds to choose features can make the final improvement optimistic; independent spatial validation is needed before operational use.

Part 1: Outcome and reliability

1A: Pull the outcome and baseline predictors
The outcome is B08013_001, aggregate travel time, divided by B08303_001, workers who did not work at home. It describes commuters aged 16 and over; people working at home are outside this denominator. A transportation agency could identify areas where commutes are longer than tract characteristics suggest.       commuters = "B08303_001", median_income = "B19013_001",
      pop_25_plus = "B15003_001", bachelors = "B15003_022",
      masters = "B15003_023", professional = "B15003_024",
      doctorate = "B15003_025", occupied_units = "B25003_001",
      renter_occupied = "B25003_003"),
    year = 2023, survey = "acs5", output = "wide", geometry = TRUE)
